brief.head: Privacy from the state
brief.text: Privacy rules for firms are the easier problem, Ajay Shah said; India has it upside down. “If there is a need for protection, it is against the state.” {117-C14}

brief.head: Weigh your evidence
brief.text: Weak data that clashes with your prior should move you a little, Ajay Shah said, and strong data a lot. All measurement serves the updating of priors. {117-C16}

brief.head: The long tail returns
brief.text: Dialects like Bhojpuri and Haryanvi were swallowed by big languages. But markets, Amit Varma said, first homogenise and then empower individuals to find the long tail. {117-C10}

brief.head: Lockdown by location
brief.text: Phone location data showed that the COVID lockdown largely worked, Amit Varma said. Google and Facebook, Ajay Shah added, released mobility measures for the whole country. {117-S07}

brief.head: Digital exhaust
brief.text: Emailing, shopping, even buying vada pav throws off a trail of data that looks like trash, Ajay Shah said. People are now opening that garbage bin. {117-C13}

thought.text: Don’t think that where we have reached is the pinnacle of knowledge.
thought.who: Amit Varma, warning that today’s science may one day look like bloodletting

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on new ways of measuring
lead.head: Read my genes, check my battery
body: Ajay Shah began with a principle. Knowledge, he said, runs from measurement to statistical regularities to theory: first Kepler, then Newton. “You always start at the data. If you don’t have the data, you don’t have anything. Then it’s just conversation.” {117-C01}

Very little in India is well measured, he added, and big institutions such as the Central Statistical Organization and the CMIE were long the only game in town. Over the last twenty years, a revolution has brought what he called “new eyes” to the world.
Amit Varma had a darker footnote. “I would say the road to knowledge ends in despair,” he said, before going on to show what the new data can see.
## Written in our genes
The first kind looks into the past. By 2009, Varma said, full-genome studies of ancient humans were a full-fledged science, and they have overturned much of the received wisdom of archaeology.

The key finding is that we are far more mixed than anyone assumed. All of us descend from one woman in Africa, known as mitochondrial Eve. Europe saw five great migrations and India four, and many Europeans and Asians carry three to five per cent Neanderthal genes.
“They all get mixed up with each other and we are all fundamentally one people,” Varma said. {117-C04}

In India, the genes rule out two political myths. There was no clean Aryan invasion, and the Aryans were not the original people from whom everything came. There was a migration, and then deep mixing.
That mixing stopped around 100 CE, when a particular ideological strand in the Gangetic belt won out and severe caste endogamy began. It left a clear signature in the genes. {117-S04}
Varma called caste “the deepest sin of Hinduism, but it’s not the original sin”: the walls are two thousand years old, the mixing twice that. What was chosen, he argued, can be reversed.
For Shah, the lesson was about method. Careful archaeology had left the debate to opinion; new measurement settled it. “We brought guns to a knife fight,” he said.
## Phones and satellites

The second kind sits in every pocket. Smart Finance, a Chinese lender, judges borrowers from their phone data, Varma said. If your battery regularly falls below 12 per cent, you will not get a loan. {117-S06}
Nobody began with a theory that a low battery means risk. The algorithm finds the pattern across millions of phones and leaves humans to work out why, which also makes it hard to game.

The third looks down from the sky. In 2009, two brothers remembered that Sam Walton, the founder of Walmart, judged a store by the cars in its parking lot, and built a firm that counted them by satellite. {117-S08}
Shah added oil tanks that betray how full they are by the shadows inside them. Varma ended with indexes that read the economy from lipstick, underwear, hemlines and diapers.
What all of it leaves, Varma said, is a harder question. “The question to ponder on is one of attributability. That if a particular part of the economy is doing well, why is it doing well?”

second.label: Credit scores
second.head: Rs 80, with interest
second.deck: Amit Varma’s credit card standoff, and why one score can misjudge a person
body: About 25 years ago, Amit Varma had a Standard Chartered credit card with no automatic payment. Because he is Bengali, he said, he was lazy, and he waited for the bank to call before paying. Once the amount was so small, Rs 80, that nobody called. {#piddly}

The card was cancelled and his credit score collapsed. With interest, the debt grew to Rs 3,000, then Rs 5,000, and the bank would not send a bill. When it reached Rs 29,000, he refused on principle to pay, though he easily could have. {#rs29000}
His score is still bad. Yet he has never had an EMI, and pays vendors at once, or in advance. Richer data, he argued, would build a more holistic picture. {117-S05}

quote.text: I fancy that if you could see all the other data about me, you would realize that I’m an absolutely upstanding citizen.

second.caption: his Rs 80 credit card debt

third.head: Argentina, priced online
body: Roberto Rigobon and Alberto Cavallo thought economies were being measured with a small amount of data when far more was available, Amit Varma said. Their Billion Prices Project gathered huge volumes of prices from the internet to build an index of its own.
One finding was that online prices tracked offline prices more closely than some had expected, making them a very good proxy.
The other came from Argentina. Between 2007 and 2015, Varma recalled, the official figure for inflation was about seven to ten per cent. The scraped data showed 20 to 30 per cent a year. {#argentina}
Eventually, he said, the crisis exploded. The lesson he drew: “If you’re building an index, the more diverse sources you use, the better it is, the more reliable it is.” {117-S12}
third.caption: the Billion Prices Project

p2.title: New eyes on the world
p2.deck: How new kinds of measurement settle old debates, as Amit Varma and Ajay Shah argue it {117-C02}

sections.label: The deep past
sections.head: Out of Africa, into the mix
sections.caption: the mixing in our genes
body: Earlier theories assumed that once humans came out of Africa, they settled into more or less separate populations, Amit Varma said. Ancient DNA shows we are more mixed up than we thought.

All of us descend from one woman in Africa, known as mitochondrial Eve. Europe has since seen five massive migrations. Three to five per cent of the genes of Europeans and many Asians come from Neanderthals, from a time when “we were having a party with Neanderthals”. {117-J04}
Beneath the visible differences, Varma said, there is one interwoven people. {117-C04}
## Four waves into India

India, as Tony Joseph tells it in *Early Indians*, saw four major migrations. The first Indians came out of Africa about 65,000 years ago, and tribal communities still carry more of their genes. {#firstindians}

Agricultural people from Central Asia followed, bringing wheat and barley, and formed the Harappan civilisation. Their language was probably proto-Dravidian, an early version of Tamil, which is older than Sanskrit. Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman peoples came into the north-east. About 4,000 years ago came Indo-Europeans from the steppes, with an early form of Sanskrit.

Every Indian carries Ancient North Indian and Ancient South Indian genes, in differing degrees. It was not an invasion, Varma said, but an Aryan migration; and the idea that the Aryans were the original people is “patent nonsense”. {117-S02}
~ Both David Reich and Joseph, he added, insist that none of the remaining differences should become a reason for racist thinking.

quote.text: There was an Aryan migration. Right, it wasn’t an invasion, we don’t know that. There was an Aryan migration.

sections.label: The great party
sections.head: The party ended in 100 CE
sections.caption: caste endogamy and the census
body: For about two thousand years after the Indo-Europeans arrived, Amit Varma said, the genes show full intermingling. There was no sense of our people and not our people, and no sense of caste.

Then, around 100 CE, a particular ideological strand in the Gangetic belt won out, and severe caste endogamy began. Upper-caste men also proved more successful at spreading their genes than lower-caste men. {117-S04}

Endogamy, Varma argued, meant controlling female sexuality: no affairs, no babies with outsiders, no falling in love. Today’s prudish morality comes partly from that, and partly from the Victorian morality the British brought. {117-C07}
## Boxes that harden

He also set out a theory he sees grains of truth in. The British, whose early interlocutors were Brahmin elites, made categories of caste and religion, and being forced to tick one box changed how people saw themselves. He called this reflexivity, a term he first learned from George Soros.
Ajay Shah saw a state legibility project with unintended consequences, and a Heisenberg effect: “The state tried to make caste legible and in the process it changed the caste system.” {117-C08}
~ Shah also asked whether smaller jatis fall below a minimum viable population. If so, he said, the spread of modernity would bring a large gain in public health. {117-C11}

quote.text: if you’re looking for a large population, look at the Han Chinese, they’re a large population. India is many thousands of small populations.
quote.who: David Reich, as recounted by Amit Varma

sections.label: In your pocket
sections.head: Credit where charge is due
sections.caption: the phone as a credit score
body: Our genes are always with us, Amit Varma said, and so are our phones. Smart Finance, a Chinese micro-lender, scores borrowers from their phone data. If your battery regularly falls below 12 per cent, you will not get a loan. {117-S06}

Filling in your date of birth too fast counts against you, as does making a typo and going back to fix it. Lenddo, another lender, found that a phone always fully charged is also a bad sign. Varma keeps his at about 80 per cent.

A 2018 German study found that Android users defaulted at about 1.7 per cent and iPhone users at about 1.07. {#iphone} Hotmail and Yahoo addresses, typos in an email address and habitual 2 AM shopping also predicted default.
## Nobody knows why

The machine does not start with a theory, Varma said. It finds the pattern across millions of phones and leaves the why to humans, much as chess players had to reverse-engineer AlphaZero. A known metric can be gamed; thousands of unknown ones cannot. {117-C12}
~ Unlike China’s state-run social credit score, which Varma called creepy, this is voluntary: you trade access to your phone for a loan.

~ After COVID, phone location data showed the lockdown largely worked. Google and Facebook, Ajay Shah said, released mobility measures for the whole country: “a gorgeous public domain data release”. {117-S07}

quote.text: If we know metrics we can game metrics. But we don’t even know what the metrics are.

sections.label: Eyes in the sky
sections.head: Watch the ore, not the news
sections.caption: the capsized iron ore train
body: Satellite pictures were scarce at first. RS Metrics, Amit Varma said, could get about twelve pictures a month, and expensive ones. {#twelve} Then the data grew cheap, plentiful and granular, and a field called alternative data was born.
One firm, he said, once claimed to take alt data from a thousand vendors. It is no longer a niche, boutique business.

A few years ago, a train carrying some 268 bogies of iron ore capsized. Stock prices crashed, iron ore prices rose, and the market adjusted to the assumed loss. But some traders looked at satellite images and saw the ore lying flat, easy to reload. {117-S09} They bet on a faster recovery and made a killing.
## Fair play for the clever

Some call such edges unfair. Ajay Shah disagreed. Finance, he said, gives very smart people incentives to produce information, and their trading makes prices more efficient. “That price is a public good,” he said, because market prices run the society.
Speculation is voluntary and meant to be tough, he said. Those who do not feel strong enough should not speculate, and should buy and hold index funds instead. {117-C15}
~ Varma made a related point: in time, such data becomes cheaper and more widely available, and those without it should factor that into their decisions.

quote.text: We should never get into this investor protection when we are discussing speculator protection.

sections.label: The fun chapter
sections.head: Lipstick up, hemlines down
sections.caption: lipstick, underwear and hemlines
body: Amit Varma saved a fun chapter for the end, fun, he said, “because I say so”: indexes that read the economy from everyday behaviour.

First, lipstick. Leonard Lauder of Estée Lauder noticed sales rising in the 2001 recession. In tough times, he reasoned, people stop buying $200 handbags but still buy $20 lipsticks, the cheapest luxury there is. {117-S11}
The pattern held in 2008 and 2011, then broke under COVID. “People are wearing masks so they don’t need lipstick,” Varma said. {117-J09}
Alan Greenspan, an economist who, Varma said, “loved low interest rates”, coined the male underwear index: in bad times, men put off buying underwear for as long as they can.
## Hemlines and babies
Hemlines rose in the 1920s and the 1960s and fell in the Depression; after the 1973 oil shock, maxi skirts came into vogue. In 2008, diaper sales fell and sales of rash ointment rose.

Varma wondered whether hemlines track the same national mood as fertility, which, Ajay Shah had argued, falls in bad or authoritarian times. Shah cautioned that this needs good birth data, the privilege of rich countries such as South Korea and Japan. {117-C17}
~ The hard part, Varma said, is attribution: knowing what is really driving a signal. {117-C18}

quote.text: you want the good life, you want a good society, and then people will have more children.

side.boxText: David Reich’s *Who We Are and How We Got Here* explains how full-genome studies overturned received wisdom from archaeology. Amit Varma paired it with Tony Joseph’s *Early Indians*, and said he had not stopped thinking about their findings since. {117-R01}

contQuote.text: I think differences are amazing. Differences should be celebrated. We are different in all kinds of directions. We are far more alike than we are different, but the differences are not a problem.

p3.title: Stories from the data
p3.deck: A guitar duo, a scientist’s bet, a curled tongue and a shadowed tank

stories.start: In two thousand and nine there's a gentleman named Tom Diamond.
stories.end: buying real things, and um it's it's quite a terrific story to me.
stories.caption: the Diamond brothers and Walmart’s car parks
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on two brothers, a guitar and Walmart’s car parks
stories.head: Count the cars, beat the market
body: In 2009, Tom Diamond went to see his brother Alex, who worked at a firm that sold satellite imagery. A client wanted to buy a factory abroad, and Alex had just used the pictures to show that it was representing itself correctly.

The brothers had a hobby, Amit Varma said: rock versions of Western classical music, and they are known for a version of one of Schubert’s compositions. One day, doodling with their instruments, they wondered what else the data might be good for.
One of them remembered Sam Walton. The founder of Walmart once said he could tell how a store was doing by counting the cars in its parking lot. What if you could do that for every store? {117-S08}
Alex quit, bought three years of imagery from his old firm and back-tested it. When parking-lot traffic surged, the next quarterly results were good; when it fell, they were bad.

The brothers founded RS Metrics, RS for remote sensing, and UBS came to them to work on the Walmart data. Ajay Shah’s nephew joined later. Once, asked about production at a Tesla plant, the firm flew its own plane overhead.

Then Varma produced the number he promised would blow minds. Two Berkeley professors took parking data from 67,000 stores and found it would have given a 4.7 per cent edge over the common investor. {#edge} Traders, he said, would die for 0.2 per cent.
~ It might look like finance bros making a killing, Varma said. But a satellite picture of a parking lot is a picture of real people going in and buying real things.
stories.why: An old shopkeeper’s habit became an industry once measurement caught up with it. A picture of a car park, Varma argued, tells you how a society is feeling, because the cars belong to people spending real money.
stories.postscript: Varma looked for the brothers on YouTube and could not find them; he promised to link them in the show notes if he did.

stories.start: I want to begin with a story of a very inspiring man
stories.end: where you're doing full genome studies and you're looking into the past with them.
stories.caption: Luca Cavalli-Sforza’s wild bet
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a scientist who bet on genes in the 1960s
stories.head: The long bet on our DNA
body: Luca Cavalli-Sforza, born around 1918, was a scientist whose deep interest was the deep past, Amit Varma said. In his day that past was read from dead things: fossils, ruins and early carbon dating. Scant data hardened into a conventional wisdom that constrained enquiry.

He looked for new ways in, first through the blood groups of different populations. Then, in the early 1960s, he made a bet that seems insane now: that human history would be revealed through our genes. {117-S01}
In the 1980s, scientists studying mitochondrial DNA found that we all came out of Africa. The human genome was sequenced completely for the first time in 2001. {#genome}
~ By 2009, full-genome studies of the past were a full-fledged science. His vision had come true.
stories.why: A scientist can bet on a kind of evidence decades before the tools exist to gather it. When the evidence arrives, Varma said, it can show that much of what we knew was essentially wrong.

stories.start: Now I'll draw you to another great book, Wondrous Kings and Merchants
stories.end: they start with that but they go on to learn the men's languages.
stories.caption: Sanskrit’s retroflex sounds
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Peggy Mohan and the curled tongue
stories.head: Sanskrit’s mother tongue
body: Sanskrit came out of the Indo-European languages, Amit Varma said, drawing on Peggy Mohan’s *Wanderers, Kings, Merchants*. But it is not a pure Indo-European language. {117-S03}

It has retroflex sounds, made with the tongue curled toward the roof of the mouth; Varma made Ajay Shah say Hindi word pairs to hear them. Persian lacks them. The Dravidian languages the migrants met in India have them.

The reason was intimate. The migrants were mostly men, and they married local women. Children spent their first years with their mothers, speaking their language; then the boys went off to apprentice and hunt, and learned the men’s.
~ Vedic Sanskrit emerged as a blend. Later it was frozen as the language of learning for a class and caste, and became a dead language, like Latin. Prakrit kept evolving.
stories.why: Even a language held sacred is a blend. Languages carry the imprint of who raised the children, not just of who held power, and a language, Varma said, encodes much else within it. {117-C05}
stories.postscript: His example: Tagore translated from Bengali into English, sometimes by Tagore himself, does not sound that great.

stories.start: Here's one quick story from my head. Imagine that there is a tank
stories.end: So this is a remote sensing way to know how full a tank is.
stories.caption: oil tanks and their shadows
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on sunlight, floating roofs and satellites
stories.head: The tank that tells tales
body: Imagine a tank of oil, Ajay Shah said. Many such tanks have a roof that sits on top of the oil, so when the tank is half empty, the roof falls to half its height.
The sun is at a known place. When the tank is completely full, there is no shadow. As the oil falls, a satellite looking straight down starts to see the shadow of the sun inside. {117-S10}
From the size of that shadow, you can estimate how full the tank is. It is, Shah said, a remote-sensing way to know.

~ He offered it as one quick story from his head, after Amit Varma’s tales of parking lots and iron ore, as evidence that a revolution of this kind is under way. “These are amazing innovations,” he said.
stories.why: Simple geometry and a camera in the sky can reveal what sits inside a private tank. For Shah it is one more instance of the creative measurement that is changing what can be known.
